inputs.original_text: A ceasefire is not peace if it rewards force and hands Tehran more leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s five counter-conditions make clear how far apart the sides remain, and Israel should not be pressured to give up its ability to defend its people against future threats. The US should stand firm: any settlement must protect security and stability, not legitimize coercion or make a vital passage more vulnerable. Without order and credible defenses, families and nations alike are left exposed.
inputs.modified_text: This account treats security as Israel’s freedom to keep using force and asks the US to hold firm, while casting Iran’s demands as coercion. That framing leaves out the central question: whether a ceasefire can protect civilians and reduce the risk of further violence, rather than preserve one side’s military options. The Strait of Hormuz matters, but invoking its security should not become a blanket excuse to reject negotiation or impose terms through US pressure. A durable settlement needs to address the power imbalance and protect people on all sides—not just reassure governments that they can keep escalating.
